title: Bram and the Postcard Again
premise: Vesper Sterling, a ghostwriter who once destroyed his own career testifying against his mentor, is hired to anonymously ghostwrite the memoirs of his old friend-turned-rival, Julian Marsh. The publisher's gimmick — pairing each memoirist with an anonymous pen-pal — misfires when the letters meant for Julian's pen-pal are routed to Vesper instead, and the handwriting on the other side belongs to Marisol Vega, the festival organizer whose life Julian's memoir will rewrite. As the Harvest Letters Festival approaches, Vesper must decide whether to protect his anonymity, expose Julian's fabrications, or confess that the man Marisol has been falling for on paper is the coward in the mirror. He ends the festival by publishing the truth under his own name, losing the commission but winning the right to be known.
about_author: Ada Okonkwo is a former court stenographer who spent a decade transcribing other people's confessions before writing her own stories. She lives in a coastal town that hosts one letter festival a year and writes the rest of the time.

chapters.title: Twelve Safe Years
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. He takes the memoir commission out of financial desperation, telling himself it's just another job. Flashback hints at the testimony that ended his career. Emotional beat: a man who has made smallness a virtue feels the walls of it tightening.

chapters.title: The Assignment Clause
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. The publisher reveals the pen-pal gimmick: memoirists exchange anonymous letters with a stranger for eight weeks, letters to be read aloud at the festival. Vesper signs, certain anonymity is the one thing he's good at. Beat: ironic confidence.

chapters.title: First Letter, Wrong Hand
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She receives her first pen-pal letter and answers it honestly, unaware the routing has failed — her letters are reaching Vesper, not her intended partner. Beat: the warmth of being unknown, which the reader knows is already compromised.

chapters.title: Julian Marsh, In His Own Words
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Interviewing Julian, Vesper hears the mentor recasting their shared history, erasing the scandal Vesper went to prison-adjacent ruin over. Beat: old fury, newly dangerous because he can't show it.

chapters.title: What Marisol Lost
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Preparing the festival, she recalls how Julian's bestselling book took credit for her family's letterpress workshop and her late brother's designs. Her letters to her pen-pal sharpen. Beat: grief converting into purpose.

chapters.title: Correspondence
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The letter exchange deepens; Vesper, answering as the anonymous pal, finds himself confessing things he's never said aloud. Marisol begins to recognize the rhythm of his sentences. Beat: intimacy built on a fault line.

chapters.title: The Handwriting on the Envelope
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She matches a phrase from her pen-pal's letter to a draft page of Julian's memoir that Vesper left in the workshop. Suspicion plants. Beat: the pleasure of the correspondence curdling into dread.

chapters.title: A Test in Ink
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She writes a deliberate trap — a false memory only Vesper would recognize — and waits. Beat: the quiet violence of testing someone you want to trust.

chapters.title: Caught by a Comma
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. He answers the trap without thinking, then rereads her letter and understands what he's done. He considers fleeing the commission. Beat: panic and the first real temptation toward honesty.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Letterpress
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She confronts Vesper privately; he admits the ghostwriting but not his past. She demands he help her stop Julian's memoir or she exposes him. Beat: enemies bound by a shared secret, alliance of necessity.

chapters.title: Digging in the Archive
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Together they search the workshop archives for proof that Julian stole the designs — old correspondence, a dated proof sheet. Beat: reluctant partnership turning into real regard.

chapters.title: Julian's Countermove
chapters.summary: Julian's POV (single chapter). He learns of the alliance and reveals he knows exactly who Vesper is and what Vesper testified to twelve years ago. He offers Vesper silence in exchange for a finished, flattering manuscript. Beat: the past arriving with a price tag.

chapters.title: The Man in the Mirror
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Alone, Vesper confronts the truth he's dodged: he didn't just testify against corruption, he enabled it for years first. His forgiveness project begins here, and it is brutal. Beat: the novel's moral hinge.

chapters.title: What the Letters Were For
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She rereads all the letters and realizes the man on the page and the man in her workshop have been the same all along — and that she cared for both. Beat: anger and tenderness refusing to separate.

chapters.title: Deadline Week
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Julian's manuscript deadline and the festival collide. Vasper drafts two endings: the lie Julian paid for, and the truth that will end him. Beat: compressed, ticking-clock tension.

chapters.title: The Stolen Proof Sheet
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Julian, tipped off, breaks into the workshop to destroy the proof sheet; Marisol catches him, and the struggle is witnessed. The town's festival committee demands answers before the festival opens. Beat: public stakes ignite.

chapters.title: Offered a Way Out
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Julian offers Vesper a final deal: finish the memoir, keep the money, keep the anonymity — the safe life, upgraded. Vesper walks out without answering. Beat: the temptation at its most seductive.

chapters.title: Night Before the Festival
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Marisol and Vesper meet among the festival lanterns; he tells her about the twelve years, the testimony, the shame. She doesn't forgive him yet, but she stays. Beat: raw confession, unearned grace.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. At the festival's letter reading, Julian presents the memoir's fabricated chapter as fact. The crowd — including the committee — turns to the anonymous pen-pals. Beat: the trap of silence closing on everyone.

chapters.title: Vesper Sterling, By Name
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Climax. Vesper takes the stage, discards his anonymity, and reads his own letter — the confession of what he did, what Julian did, and what the proof sheet shows. He surrenders the commission and the fee in front of everyone. Beat: the cost of the mirror finally paid.

chapters.title: After the Applause Dies
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Consequences: the publisher withdraws Julian's memoir, the committee authenticates the workshop's claim, Vesper faces professional ruin and finds he can bear it. Marisol asks him to stay through the season — as himself. Beat: justice outside the courts, belonging without a mask.

chapters.title: A Letter Worth Keeping
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV, epilogue. Months later, Vesper writes under his own name for the first time; the last page of the book is the first letter of a new correspondence, signed. Beat: quiet, earned hope — identity kept, not rebuilt.
